item.title: Former NY Fed President on Remembering 9/11
item.description: [Bloomberg] William Dudley discussed Dudley’s experience on a diverted flight during the FAA ground stop after the attacks. Dudley said the plane was unable to land in the U.S. and was sent to Saint John’s, Newfoundland, where passengers were kept for six days. He compared the experience to the musical Come From Away, saying it accurately captured what stranded travelers went through. Dudley recalled the uncertainty at first, including the pilot’s refusal to explain what was happening until they were on the ground, but emphasized the generosity of Canadians who housed, fed, and clothed the stranded passengers. The conversation also reflected on the tragedy of Sept. 11, honoring first responders and noting that, despite the horror of the attacks, many people rose to the occasion with heroism and kindness. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: KBW CEO on re-building Manhattan after 9/11
item.description: [Bloomberg] Tom Michaud describes how KBW responded in the aftermath of Sept. 11 by focusing first on helping the families of victims and then on rebuilding the firm. He says he, John Duffy, and Andy Senczak formed the top leadership group, alongside an office of the chairman, and that nearly all of the firm’s colleagues came from the equity side. Michaud says the rebuilding effort gave the team a way to channel grief and energy into action, and he recalls the determination that KBW could not end because of the attacks. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Former NYC Deputy Mayor on Remembering 9/11
item.description: [Bloomberg] Edward Skyler reflects on the aftermath of 9/11, saying it was extremely difficult to make decisions in the wake of a tragedy that left 2,700 people murdered and the city filled with grief, anxiety, and political tension. He recalls that when Mayor Bloomberg was sworn in on 01/01/2002, smoke was still rising from the World Trade Center site and the economic damage had already been done. Skyler says the period was marked by intense emotions and strong voices from people opposed to New York, and that the job of city leaders was to listen to all sides and develop a plan that served the city’s best interests, even if it disappointed some people. He concludes that, in hindsight, those decisions have stood the test of time. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Rebuilding After 9/11, Cantor Fitzgerald's Annual Charity, Eye on Energy Markets

Ed Morse Hartree Partners Senior Advisor And Commodities analyst, Brandon Lutnick, Cantor Fitzgerald Chariman and Kyle Lutnick Cantor Fitzgerald Vice Chariman. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: SL Green CFO on Lower Manhattan's rebound after 9/11
item.description: [Bloomberg] Matt DiLiberto discussed the 25-year transformation of Lower Manhattan after Sept. 11, saying the area has been “reimagined” from a largely nine-to-five financial district into a vibrant neighborhood where people live, work, study, and visit. He said the central question after the attacks was not whether the area would be rebuilt, but how, how long it would take, who would do it, and what it would ultimately look like. DiLiberto pointed to the area’s growth in population and housing, along with a mix of office space and memorialization around the World Trade Center site. From SL Green’s perspective, he said the company focused more on residential projects in the area because of how the neighborhood evolved, citing developments such as 100 Church Street, 33 Beekman, and 180 Broadway. He framed the redevelopment as part of a broader need for New York to remain strong and vibrant not just in Midtown, but downtown as well. (Source: Bloomberg)
